setting: a language-learning platform for corporate teams (Lumen Learning)
prompt: I’m preparing a pitch for Maya Patel, our Chief Product Officer, about rolling out an AI‑driven conversation coach on Lumen Learning. We have 20,000 corporate users as of June 2024, and the pilot in Q1 2024 showed a 12% increase in weekly active minutes. The proposal is to license the AI model for $0.018 per minute of usage, which we estimate will cost $450k annually based on an assumed 250 minutes per user per month. We also plan to price the new feature as a $12 per seat add‑on, expecting a 15% uptake among existing accounts by March 1 2025, generating $360k in incremental revenue. The key assumption is that the corporate discount tier will not erode our gross margin. What we don’t know is the churn impact after introducing the coach—early feedback suggests some admins may drop the platform if the AI feels intrusive. I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, outline the main ways this could fail (including any arithmetic or cost‑risk slip you spot), and state the pre‑agreed condition that would make us kill the rollout.

setting: a solar-installer lead-generation site (Sunrow Leads)
prompt: I’m the lead of growth at Sunrow Leads and I have a draft pitch for Maya Patel, our CEO, to get approval for a new lead‑generation funnel. The plan is to launch a paid‑search campaign on July 15, 2024, aiming for 12,000 qualified solar‑installer leads per month at an estimated $15 per lead. We expect an 8 % conversion to paid contracts, which would generate roughly $2.5 M in revenue by the end of Q4 2025. The assumption is that the conversion rate will stay constant even as we scale. We’ve benchmarked against GreenGrid’s Q2 2023 numbers—30 % higher lead volume—but they ran a 6‑month pilot while we plan a full rollout in just 3 months. I don’t know the churn rate after the first twelve months, and I haven’t priced the compliance cost for the new federal solar tax credit reporting requirements (likely a few hundred thousand dollars). Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to push this forward, list the main ways the plan could fail (including any arithmetic or comparison issues you spot), and tell me the specific result that would trigger us to kill or pivot the initiative. The answer is for Maya Patel.

setting: a SaaS tool for wedding planners (Evermore Planner)
prompt: I’m preparing a pitch for Lila Nguyen, our CEO, about rolling out a new automated vendor‑matching module in Evermore Planner. The idea is to launch on 2024‑09‑01, integrate with three major bridal‑venue APIs, and charge a $20 premium per month to the 12,000 active planners we have now. We estimate $1.2 million annual recurring revenue (12,000 × $100 × 12 months × 10% uptake) and claim it will cut planner churn by 10% (our current churn is 8% per year). The development contract is $150,000, plus a $30,000 yearly maintenance fee, and we’re assuming the APIs will stay at current pricing. The unknown is the latency and reliability of the third‑party calendar service, which could affect real‑time booking sync. I need you to give Lila a single recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the three biggest ways this could fail (technical, financial, or market‑adoption), and define the pre‑agreed condition that would make us kill the project—specifically, the metric or event that would trigger a stop‑go decision. Thanks.

setting: a regional bus operator piloting on-demand shuttles (Harbor Transit)
prompt: I’m the VP of Operations at Harbor Transit, and I need a quick stress‑test of the on‑demand shuttle pilot before I present it to our CEO, Maya Patel, next week. We plan to add 12 electric shuttles to the existing 45‑bus fleet, rolling them out in three waves starting 2024‑03‑01, with a total capital outlay of $2.1 million and an estimated operating cost of $150 k per shuttle per year. The goal is a 10 % lift in weekday ridership (about 4,800 additional boardings) and a 3 % reduction in overall fuel expense by the end of the 18‑month pilot. I’m assuming a 70 % adoption rate of the on‑demand app among our regular riders within the first six months. The unknown is the regulatory fee for adding service zones in two new municipalities, which the city council has not yet finalized. Also, our cost‑per‑ride comparison uses a competitor’s $5 average fare but ignores their higher mileage subsidy, so the arithmetic may be off. Please give me one clear recommendation, the three biggest ways this could fail, and the specific result (e.g., <2 % ridership lift after 9 months) that would trigger us to kill or pivot the pilot.

setting: an online used-textbook marketplace (Quill Exchange)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test a proposal I’m taking to Ellen Park, our CEO, for a new “Rapid‑Match” service on Quill Exchange. The idea is to add an algorithm that instantly pairs sellers with buyers based on course codes, promising to boost conversions from the current 12% to 18% within six months (by September 1, 2025). We estimate the service will generate $1.2 million in incremental revenue in the first year, with direct costs of $800 k (including $200 k for server upgrades and $150 k for marketing that we left out of the original spreadsheet). The plan assumes we can attract 5,000 new active users per month after launch. A competitor, TextTrade, is rumored to cut its transaction fee from 12% to 8% next quarter—a real unknown we can’t verify. I want one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the three biggest ways this could fail, and the specific result that would trigger us to kill the project (e.g., if monthly active users don’t exceed 3,500 by month 4). Also watch for any arithmetic or cost gaps in my numbers.

setting: a cybersecurity training startup selling to schools (Northgate Secure)
prompt: Maya Patel here, VP of Sales at Northgate Secure. I’m preparing a pitch for our COO, Ethan Reyes, about rolling out a new gamified phishing‑simulation product for K‑12 districts. The plan is to price the service at $8 per student per year, target 12,000 students in the first quarter, and announce a pilot starting 1 May 2025 with three midsize districts. We’ve budgeted $150,000 for development, $30,000 for the Q1 marketing push, and $40,000 for a dedicated support team, but we haven’t factored any integration licensing fees yet. I’m assuming each school will allocate at least $0.10 per student from their cybersecurity budget, which would let us hit $96,000 in revenue in Q1 (12,000 × $8). Our competitor SecureLearn charges $12 per student and claims 40 % higher engagement, but we haven’t validated that claim. The real unknown is how many districts will be forced to meet the new state cybersecurity compliance deadline of 31 July 2025. Could you give me one recommendation on whether to move forward, the main ways this rollout could fail, and the specific result that would trigger us to kill or pivot the project? Thanks.

setting: a meal-kit company for athletes (Stride Kitchen)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal to present to Maya Patel, our CFO, next Tuesday and need it stress‑tested. We plan to launch a “Performance Boost” line of high‑protein meal kits aimed at endurance athletes. The pilot would run for 8 weeks starting 15 Oct 2025, covering 12,000 meals at an estimated $2.7 per meal, which I’ve rounded to a $30k total ingredient budget (I’m assuming the rounding is acceptable). We expect a 5% conversion to a 6‑month subscription at $120 per customer, which should generate roughly $108k in revenue. The marketing spend is set at $25k for targeted social ads and partnerships with three local gyms, each paying $8k for co‑branding. I’m assuming the gyms will deliver at least 500 qualified leads each. The unknown is the churn rate after the pilot and whether the $2.7 cost per meal truly includes packaging waste disposal, which we haven’t priced yet. Please give me: one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the three most likely ways this plan could fail, and the specific trigger (e.g., churn >12% or cost per meal exceeding $3) that would make us stop or pivot. Thanks.

setting: a property-management app for small landlords (Rowan Rentals)
prompt: Maya, our CEO, wants me to pitch a new automated lease‑renewal module for Rowan Rentals. We have 1,200 active landlords who currently list an average of 2.4 units each, and the average rent collected is $1,250 per month. The product team estimates the module will add $35 k in monthly recurring revenue by year 2, based on a $5 per unit per month surcharge that we think 70 % of landlords will accept. Development is budgeted at $250 k, with a 90‑day build window and a $30 k marketing push. We assume the churn rate will stay at the historic 5 % annually, and that the new feature won’t affect the existing customer support load. The unknown is the actual willingness to pay the $5 surcharge—our survey only covered 50 landlords and showed mixed results. I need you to give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, list the three biggest ways this could fail (including any hidden costs or risks you spot), and tell me the specific result that would trigger us to kill the project under the pre‑agreed condition we set (e.g., if the pilot conversion falls below a certain threshold).

setting: a podcast hosting and ad-insertion company (Echo Harbor)
prompt: I’m pulling together the briefing for Maya Patel, our CEO, about switching Echo Harbor’s ad‑insertion platform from the current static system to the AI‑driven dynamic engine PulseWave offered. The plan calls for a $1.2 million upfront integration fee plus a $150,000 monthly license. We expect a 20 % lift in CPM from $3.50 to $4.20, which on our average 150,000 monthly listeners would add roughly $1.5 million in incremental revenue over the first 12 months. Our current ad‑revenue for 2023 was $6.3 million, with a churn rate of 4 % each quarter. The assumption is we can complete the rollout in 8 weeks using our existing five‑engineer dev team, so we won’t need any new hires. The unknown is the actual CPM uplift once the personalized ads go live – we have no pilot data. I need you to give Maya one clear recommendation (go ahead, pause, or scrap), list the three biggest ways this could fail, and state the pre‑agreed kill condition: if net incremental profit after the first six months is under $250,000, we should stop and revert. Also watch for any hidden cost or logic error in the financials.

setting: a dental-supply e-commerce business (Brightside Dental Supply)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal to roll out a subscription service for Brightside Dental Supply’s consumables and need it stress‑tested before I present it to our CEO, Maya Patel. The plan is to launch the pilot on Jan 15 2025 with 100 existing customers, giving them a 15 % discount on monthly kits that include gloves, masks, and prophylaxis paste. We project $2.1 M in revenue in the first 12 months, with $1.2 M in direct costs (including $200 k for the new logistics partner, $300 k for packaging, and $250 k for software integration). We assume 30 % of our 12,000 current customers will convert within the first year, giving us a break‑even point at 18 months. The only real unknown is how the logistics partner’s API latency will affect order processing during peak weeks. I also compared our expected churn (5 %) to Competitor DentalCo’s 5 % churn, but didn’t adjust for the fact they sell only single‑use items. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, outline the three most likely ways this could fail, and tell me the specific result (e.g., if pilot net profit falls below $150 k after six months) that should trigger us to kill or pivot the idea.

setting: a clinical-trial recruitment platform (Meridian Trials)
prompt: Jordan Patel, our CEO, will see this next week. I’m proposing we invest $150,000 to build an AI‑driven matching engine for Meridian Trials that promises to cut the average recruitment cycle from 45 days to about 31 days – a 30 % speed‑up. We run roughly four trials a year, each worth $5 M in revenue, and I’m assuming that shaving 14 days per trial translates directly into $500k extra revenue per quarter (the same $5 M divided by 12 months, then multiplied by the 30 % gain). The development would be done in three months, after which we’d need a six‑month integration window before pilots start. I need you to give Jordan one clear recommendation: go ahead, hold, or scrap. Also lay out the three biggest ways this could fail, and tell me the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us stop or pivot – for example if the integration drags beyond six months or the net revenue lift falls below $200k per quarter. The unknown is the regulatory approval timeline for the AI module; we haven’t priced any additional compliance costs. Please keep the answer concise and focused on the decision.

setting: a ride-share bike maker adding a rental fleet (Cobalt Cycles)
prompt: I’m drafting a proposal to add a dedicated bike‑rental fleet for Cobalt Cycles and need it stress‑tested before I present it to our COO, Maya Patel, next week. We plan to purchase 100 e‑bikes at $1,200 each, allocate $120 k for a depot, and spend $30 k on a mobile app update. The model assumes each bike will log 150 rides per month at $3 per ride, giving $450 k in monthly revenue, and we’ve budgeted 30 % of revenue for maintenance and charging. The rollout is slated for Q1 2025, with break‑even expected in month 10. I’m assuming rider churn will mirror our current subscription service (5 % monthly), but we don’t yet know the insurance premium for a fleet of this size. Also, I compared the projected $540 k annual revenue to a car‑sharing service that earns $600 k with only 80 vehicles, which may be an apples‑to‑oranges comparison. Please give me: one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and the specific metric (e.g., cumulative net loss > $200 k by month 8) that would trigger us to kill or pivot the initiative.

setting: an e-signature tool for freelancers (Penstroke)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test before I pitch this to Maya Patel, our CFO, next Tuesday. Penstroke now has 12,000 active freelancers, each generating an average contract value of $1,200, and we’re seeing an 8% churn per quarter. I’m proposing we add an AI‑driven contract‑suggestion module that will cost a $75,000 upfront development fee plus $2,000 a month for cloud hosting. We estimate it will lift our conversion rate by 15% and cut manual processing time, saving roughly $5,000 each month. My core assumption is that at least 75% of our freelancers will start using the feature within the first six months. The unknown is how the new data‑privacy regulations coming into effect on 1 November 2026 might affect our architecture and whether we’ll need additional compliance work. I want you to give me: one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, the main ways this rollout could fail (including any hidden cost or risk you spot), and the pre‑agreed kill condition – i.e., the result that would make us stop or pivot the project. Please keep the answer focused on the CFO’s perspective.

setting: a farm-equipment leasing marketplace (Greenfurrow Leasing)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the “Premium Tractor‑as‑a‑Service” rollout I’m taking to our COO, Maya Patel, next week. We plan to launch a pilot on 15 September 2024 with 300 farms in the Midwest, each taking a 24‑month lease priced at $4,500 per month, which I’ve tallied as $1.2 million in revenue (300 × 4,500 × 12 = $1.62 M, but I’m using the 12‑month figure). Our cost estimate is $800 k for acquisition, $120 k for insurance, and $70 k for support, leaving a projected net of $310 k. We assume the average utilization will be 85 % and that the market will grow 15 % YoY. The unknown is the actual churn rate after the first year; we have no data beyond our three‑month pilot. Please give me a single recommendation on whether to proceed, outline the three biggest ways this could fail (including any hidden cost or assumption you spot), and specify the pre‑agreed condition that would make us abort the program (e.g., if net cash flow falls below a certain threshold). The answer is for Maya, so keep it concise and executive‑ready.

setting: a museum ticketing and membership platform (Atlas Arts Pass)
prompt: Hi, I need you to stress‑test a plan I’m about to take to Maya Patel, our CEO, for the Atlas Arts Pass platform. Right now we have 22,000 active members paying $60 annually. I’m proposing a premium tier at $120 per year, promising unlimited entry to all special exhibitions and a 15 % discount on museum shop purchases. We expect 12 % of the current base (about 2,640 members) to upgrade within the next 12 months, which I calculated would generate an extra $316,800 in revenue. I’m assuming an 80 % renewal rate for the premium tier and that the discount will increase shop sales by $5 per member per month. The integration with our ticketing system is quoted at $40,000, but we haven’t added the $15,000 cost for staff training and the $7,500 for a third‑party analytics add‑on. The real unknown is the churn rate for the new tier after the first year. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to move forward, list the three main ways this could fail, and state the pre‑agreed condition (e.g., if the pilot’s net profit margin falls below 5 % after six months) that would trigger us to kill the idea. Thank you.

setting: a boutique fitness studio chain adding an app (Juniper Studios)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the app rollout plan I’m about to present to Maya Patel, our CEO, and I want you to give me one clear recommendation, the three biggest ways this could flop, and the specific trigger that would make us kill the project. We have 12 Juniper Studios locations with 8,500 active members as of 1 May 2024. The proposal is to spend $120 k on development, $30 k a year on maintenance, and another $20 k on marketing, launching in Q3 2025. I’m assuming 60 % of members will download and use the app within the first six months, which should drive a 15 % lift in overall revenue (about $1.5 M) and reduce class‑booking admin time by 2 hours per studio per week. The unknown is the exact integration cost with our legacy CRM – the vendor only gave a ballpark of $10‑$15 k. Also, we haven’t priced the potential churn impact if the app experience is sub‑par. I think the numbers look solid, but I’m uneasy about the $150 k total first‑year cost I quoted (I may have missed the marketing spend) and the fact we’re comparing our projected lift to a competitor’s 20 % increase without adjusting for their twice‑the‑size member base. Tell me if this makes sense, what could go wrong, and what adoption figure (e.g., under 30 % after three months) would be the kill switch.

setting: a municipal parking-permit software vendor (Acme Civic Tech)
prompt: Hi, I'm Maya, product lead at Acme Civic Tech. I need to brief the city's Deputy Mayor, Carlos Ruiz, on the proposal to replace the existing parking‑permit platform with our new SaaS solution. The current system handles 72,000 permits per year, costs $120,000 annually to maintain, and requires a $15,000 yearly upgrade fee. Our new platform promises a 30% reduction in operational cost and a $200,000 one‑time implementation fee, plus a $75,000 integration cost with the legacy GIS that we haven't priced yet. I’m assuming the city will adopt the new system for at least 3 years and that the projected 30% savings will materialize immediately. The unknown is the exact date the GIS team can provide the required API specs; they said “by early Q3 2025” but gave no firm commitment. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, list the main ways this rollout could fail, and tell me the pre‑agreed condition (e.g., if the first‑year savings fall short of $30,000) that would make us kill the project. Thanks.

setting: a vet clinic group testing subscription wellness plans (Pinewood Vets)
prompt: I need you to stress‑test the subscription wellness plan I'm about to pitch to Dr. Maya Patel, the owner of Pinewood Vets. The plan would roll out across our five clinics starting 1 July 2025, charging $79 per pet per month for a 12‑month commitment. We expect a 15 % churn after the first year and forecast 1,200 members in the first six months, which should generate $1.13 million in revenue (79 × 1,200 × 6). I assume the average pet will need three preventive visits per year, so we budget $45 per visit for supplies and labor. The start‑up cost is $250 k for software integration, plus an estimated $80 k in marketing spend, but we haven’t quantified the compliance cost for tele‑health consultations, which is an unknown. We compare this to competitor GreenPaws’ single‑visit $199 package, but we haven’t adjusted for the fact that GreenPaws includes a free diagnostic lab test worth $30. Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to proceed, list the three most likely ways this could fail, and tell me the specific metric (e.g., net profit below $50 k after six months) that would trigger us to kill or pivot the program.

setting: a B2B invoice-financing marketplace (Fernhill Capital Exchange)
prompt: I need a concise briefing for our CFO, Maya Patel, on whether we should launch the “Rapid Credit Line” pilot for Fernhill Capital Exchange next quarter. The pilot would let small suppliers on the platform receive financing within 24 hours of invoice upload. We plan to onboard 120 suppliers (up from the current 85) and process $4.2 million in invoices per month, with an expected 5 % default rate based on last year’s data. Our tech team says the API integration will take 6 weeks and cost $78 k in development plus $12 k per month for the new risk‑scoring engine. I’m assuming the 5 % default cost can be covered by a 0.8 % fee on financed invoices, which we think will generate $33 k in monthly revenue. The unknown is how long the regulator will take to approve the new financing product; we have no timeline yet. Please give me one clear recommendation (go forward or not), list the three biggest ways this pilot could fail, and specify the pre‑agreed trigger that would make us abort the pilot (e.g., a threshold of losses, regulatory delay, or cost overrun). Also note any hidden risk you see in the numbers or assumptions.

setting: a coffee roaster launching wholesale to offices (Bluebird Roasters)
prompt: I need a quick stress‑test of the wholesale pitch I’m taking to Julia, our co‑founder, tomorrow. We plan to launch Bluebird Roasters’ office program in Q3 2025 targeting 500 corporate locations, each receiving an average of 100 12‑oz bags per month at $25 per bag. I’ve run the numbers assuming a 3 % discount for a 12‑month contract, which gives us $1.45 M in projected revenue (I calculated 500 × 100 × 12 × $25 × 0.97). Our cost per bag is $12 for beans, $3 for packaging, and $2 for shipping, so I’m quoting a gross margin of about 52 %. I’m also budgeting $120 k for a “launch marketing” push and $80 k for a coffee‑machine lease program that we think will boost adoption. The assumption is that office coffee consumption will stay flat despite the recent work‑from‑home trend. The unknown is the actual take‑rate: we have no firm data on how many offices will sign up after the first quarter. Please give me: one clear recommendation on whether to go ahead, the three biggest ways this plan could fail, and the specific metric (e.g., <30 % of targeted offices signing contracts after 3 months) that would trigger us to kill or pivot the initiative.
